_note: Original advanced lesson. Uses language-specific block variants where syntax differs.
title: Stacks & Queues
summary: Use a **stack** when the newest item should come out first. Use a **queue** when the oldest item should come out first.
refresher: A **stack** is last-in, first-out: push adds to the top, and pop removes that same top item. A **queue** is first-in, first-out: enqueue adds to the back, and dequeue removes the oldest item from the front.
refresher_code:
stack: push A, push B, pop -> B
queue: add A, add B, remove -> A

advanced-stack-lifo.title: Stack order means newest first
advanced-stack-lifo.body: A **stack** acts like a pile. The newest item is on top, so it **leaves** first.
advanced-stack-lifo.example: push A, push B, push C, pop -> C
advanced-stack-lifo.notice: The item that **leaves** is the one most recently added.
advanced-stack-lifo.mistake: Do not remove from the front if the question says **stack**.

advanced-queue-fifo.title: Queue order means oldest first
advanced-queue-fifo.body: A **queue** acts like a line. The first item waiting is handled first.
advanced-queue-fifo.example: add A, add B, add C, remove -> A
advanced-queue-fifo.notice: Add at one end, remove from the other.
advanced-queue-fifo.mistake: Removing from the newest end turns the **queue** into a **stack**.

advanced-stack-parentheses.title: Stacks remember unfinished openings
advanced-stack-parentheses.body: When you see an opening parenthesis, push it. When you see a closing parenthesis, pop one opening.
advanced-stack-parentheses.example: ( [ ] ) works because each close matches the newest opening.
advanced-stack-parentheses.notice: Nested work closes in reverse order.
advanced-stack-parentheses.mistake: Matching a close with the oldest opening breaks nested expressions.

advanced-queue-bfs.title: Queues keep breadth-first search in order
advanced-queue-bfs.body: BFS visits all current neighbors before moving farther away. A **queue** keeps that arrival order.
advanced-queue-bfs.example: visit start, enqueue its neighbors, then remove the oldest neighbor next
advanced-queue-bfs.mistake: Using a **stack** changes the search into depth-first behavior.

sections.title: Stack: newest item first
sections.summary: A **stack** stores work so the most recent item **leaves** first.

blocks.body: A **stack** is useful when the newest unfinished thing matters first. Undo buttons, browser back history, **function** calls, and matching parentheses all use this idea.

blocks.title: Stack words you will see
items: `push` means add an item to the top.
`pop` means remove and **return** the top item.
`peek` means look at the top item without removing it.
`is_empty` means ask whether there is anything to remove.

blocks.caption: The shortest **stack** uses the end of a **list** or **array** as the top.

python.code:
stack = []
stack.append("A")   # push A
stack.append("B")   # push B on top of A
top = stack.pop()    # remove B
print(top)
print(stack)

blocks.title: Why append and pop go together
blocks.body: In Python and JavaScript, `append` or `push` adds to the end of the **list**. `pop()` removes from that same end. That pair makes the end behave like the top of the **stack**.

sections.title: Build a small Stack class
sections.summary: A **class** can wrap the **list** so the **stack** rules are easy to reuse.

blocks.body: A **stack** **class** is not magic. It is a small wrapper around storage. The wrapper gives names to the operations so the rest of your code can say `push`, `pop`, and `peek` instead of reaching into the **list** directly.

blocks.caption: A beginner-friendly **stack** implementation with each **method** doing one job.

blocks.title: Read the Python version line by line
items: `__init__` runs when a new **stack** is created. It starts with an empty **list**.
`append(item)` adds to the end. We treat that end as the top.
`pop()` removes and returns the last item.
`items[-1]` looks at the last item without removing it.
The empty check prevents a crash when there is nothing to remove.

blocks.title: Do not hide an empty pop by accident
blocks.body: Returning `None` or `null` is beginner-friendly, but real programs may throw an error instead. The important habit is checking what should happen when the **stack** is empty.

sections.title: Queue: oldest item first
sections.summary: A **queue** stores work in arrival order.

blocks.body: A **queue** is useful when the first thing waiting should be handled first. Lines at a desk, printer jobs, notifications, and breadth-first search use this idea.

blocks.caption: Add to the back. Remove from the front.

python.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("A")      # enqueue A
queue.append("B")      # enqueue B behind A
first = queue.popleft() # dequeue A
print(first)
print(list(queue))

blocks.caption: **Stack** and queue differ in which item leaves next.
blocks.wrong: Add A, add B, remove B
blocks.right: Add A, add B, remove A
blocks.body: Both structures add items. The difference is the removal rule.

blocks.title: Python queue note
blocks.body: `deque` is a good Python **queue** because removing from the left is fast. A normal **list** can do it, but `pop(0)` has to shift the remaining items.

sections.title: Trace before you code
sections.summary: Most **stack** and **queue** bugs are order bugs.

blocks.body: Before writing code, draw the structure after each operation. This catches the most common mistake: removing the right **value** from the wrong end.

blocks.prompt: A **stack** receives 10, then 20, then 30. What does the first pop **return**?
blocks.why: The newest item is 30, so a **stack** pops 30 first.

blocks.prompt: A **queue** receives 10, then 20, then 30. What does the first remove **return**?
blocks.why: The oldest item is 10, so a **queue** removes 10 first.

sections.title: Practice handoff
sections.summary: Use the operation names to choose the structure.

blocks.body: If the prompt says newest, undo, reverse, nested, or matching parentheses, think **stack** first. If it says oldest, waiting line, level order, or BFS, think **queue** first.

blocks.title: Do not memorize only the method names
blocks.body: **Method** names change by language. The rule stays the same: stack removes newest, queue removes oldest.
